abstract: Summary Peritoneal carcinomatosis (PC) in gastric adenocarcinoma (GAC) is the most common metastatic site and leads to a short median survival. Exosomes have been shown to remodel the microenvironment, facilitating tumor metastases. However, the functional component in GAC cell-derived exosomes that remodel the landscape in the peritoneal cavity remains unclear. To address this, we performed in-depth proteomic profiling of ascites-derived exosomes from patients with PC, and we found that Galectin-3 was highly enriched in exosomes derived from malignant ascites. exosomal Galectin-3 was the crucial regulator of PC. Blockage of exosomal Galectin-3 significantly inhibited tumor metastases and prolonged overall survival. Exosomal Galectin-3 activated cancer-associated fibroblasts through integrin α1β1/FAK/Akt/mTOR/CXCL12 signaling. Combined inhibition of the CXCL12-CXCR4 axis and exosomal Galectin-3 enhanced the efficacy of anti-PD-1 immunotherapy, leading to significantly diminished PC progression and durable antitumor responses. These findings provide a rationale for clinical strategy of targeting exosomal Galectin-3 to treat PC.

All cell lines were profiled, authenticated, and Mycoplasma-tested in the Cell Line Core Facility at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center every 6 months. Patient-derived orthotopic model

For the orthotopic injection, SCID mice were first anesthetized with isoflurane inhalation and then laid in a supine position. Method details
Isolation of extracellular vesicles by density gradient flotation
Microvesicles were depleted from ascite samples by centrifugation at 2000 × g for 20 minutes, followed by 16,500 × g for 30 minutes; resulting supernatant was filtered through a pre-wetted 0.22-μm vacuum filter. Microvesicle-depleted biospecimens were densified by mixing with OptiPrep iodixanol solution (Sigma D1556) to a final density of 1.16-1.30 g/mL and loaded into the bottom of a polycarbonate ultracentrifuge tube and overlaid with 0.5- to 2-mL aliquots of iodixanol/phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) solution in the 1.20-1.01 g/mL (35-0% wt/vol) range, proceeding from the highest to lowest density to form a single- or multi-step density fractionation gradient as needed. Ultracentrifugation was performed at 100,000 ×
g
for 4 hours at 8°C. Vesicles were collected from the top of the tube, proceeding downward to recover volume equal to 90% of overlaid gradient volume. Density of harvested fractions was assessed against a standard curve based on sample absorbance at 250 nm using a NanoDrop microvolume spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Wilmington, DE). Vesicle harvests were stored at -80°C.
Proteomic profiling of extracellular vesicles
ECV-derived protein digestion and identification by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry was performed using established protocols. The nanoAcquity UPLC system coupled in-line with a WATERS SYNAPT G2-Si mass spectrometer was used for the separation of pooled digested protein fractions. The system was equipped with a Waters Symmetry C18 nanoAcquity trap-column (180 μm × 20 mm, 5 μm) and a Waters HSS-T3 C18 nanoAcquity analytical column (75 μm × 150 mm, 1.8 μm). The column oven temperature was set at 50°C, and the temperature of the tray compartment in the auto-sampler was set at 6°C. LC-HDMSE data were acquired in resolution mode with SYNAPT G2-Si using Waters Masslynx (version 4.1, SCN 851). The capillary voltage was set to 2.80 kV, sampling cone voltage to 30 V, source offset to 30 V, and source temperature to 100°C. Mobility used high-purity N2 as the drift gas in the IMS TriWave cell. The pressure was 4.50 mbar in the helium cell, 2.47 × 10
−2
mbar in the Trap cell, 2.90 mbar in the IMS TriWave cell, and 2.53 × 10
−3
mbar in the Transfer cell. IMS wave velocity was 600 m/s, helium cell DC 50 V, Trap DC bias 45 V, IMS TriWave DC bias 1 V, and IMS wave delay 1000 μs. The mass spectrometer was operated in V-mode with a typical resolving power of at least 20,000. All analyses were performed using positive mode ESI using a NanoLockSpray source. The lock mass channel was sampled every 60 seconds. The mass spectrometer was calibrated with a [Glu1] fibrinopeptide solution (300 fmol/μL) delivered through the reference sprayer of the NanoLockSpray source. Accurate mass LC-HDMSE data were collected in an alternating low-energy (MS) and high-energy (MSE) mode of acquisition with mass scan ranging from 50 m/z to 1800 m/z. The spectral acquisition time in each mode was 1.0 seconds with a 0.1-second inter-scan delay. In low-energy HDMS mode, data were collected at a constant collision energy of 2 eV in both the Trap cell and the Transfer cell. In high-energy HDMSE mode, the collision energy was ramped from 25 eV to 55 eV in the Transfer cell only. The RF applied to the quadrupole mass analyzer was adjusted such that ions from 300 m/z to 2000 m/z were efficiently transmitted, ensuring that any ions observed in the LC-HDMSE data <300 m/z arose from dissociations in the Transfer collision cell. The acquired LC-HDMSE data were processed and searched against a protein knowledge database (Uniprot) through the ProteinLynx Global Server (PLGS, Waters Company) with a 4% false discovery rate.
Exosome production from GAC cell line
The cells were cultured in serum-free medium for 48 hours at a confluency of 70-80% and washed twice with PBS. The conditioned medium was collected and followed by differential centrifugation at 800 × g for 5 minutes and 2,000 × g for 10 minutes, and then filtered using a 0.2-μm filter. Exosome isolation was performed by ultracentrifugation at 100,000 × g for 3 hours at 4°C. After ultracentrifugation, the supernatant was discarded, and the pellet was resuspended in PBS.
Nanoparticle tracking analysis
The size distribution of exosomes was determined based on the Brownian motion using a NanoSight LM10 (Malvern), which is equipped with a high-sensitivity sCMOS camera and Blue488 laser. The temperature was set at 25°C during measurement of exosomes. The syringe pump speed was set to 20. A 90-second delay followed by three captures of 30 seconds each was employed for each acquisition.
Transmission electron microscopy of exosomes
Exosomes were fixed in 2.5% EM grade glutaraldehyde. Formvar-carbon coated mesh nickel grids were treated with poly-l-lysine solution for 5 minutes, and excess was removed by the filter paper. The grids were allowed to dry. Drops of suspended exosomes were deposited on the formvar-carbon coated mesh nickel grids. Exosomes were adsorbed for 1 hour at room temperature. Grids were rinsed with PBS 5 times for 3 minutes each and incubated in filtered 1% uranyl acetate in distilled water for 1 minute. The excess was removed by filter paper, and grids were allowed to dry at room temperature. Grids were examined in a JEM 1010 transmission electron microscope (JEOL, USA, Inc, Peabody, MA) at 80 kV. Digital images were captured using the AMT Imaging System (Advanced Microscopy Techniques Corp, Danvers, MA).
Flow cytometry-based analysis of bead-bound exosomes
A total of 5 × 10
9
exosomes were resuspended in 100 μL of PBS and mixed with 10 μL of aldehyde/sulfate beads (Invitrogen). Then, the samples were incubated at room temperature with rotation for 15 minutes. Subsequently, exosomes were added with 400 μL of PBS and rotated overnight at 4°C. Samples were added to 200 μL of 1M glycine and rotated at room temperature for 1 hour on the following day. The bead-bound exosomes were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 2 minutes, the supernatant was discarded, and the samples were resuspended in 100 μL of 10% bovine serum albumin (BSA) for blocking and rotated at room temperature for 1 hour. After blocking, samples were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 2 minutes, supernatant was discarded, and the precipitate was resuspended in 50 μL of 2% BSA containing unconjugated primary antibodies CD9 (BD, Cat# 558749), CD63 (BD, Cat# 564221), and CD81 (BD, Cat# 559519). The samples were rotated at room temperature for 1 hour. Bead-bound exosomes were washed twice in 200 μL of 2% BSA, followed by centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 2 minutes. The supernatant was discarded, and bead-bound exosomes were rotated for 1 hour at room temperature with 20 μL of 2% BSA containing secondary antibody. Then the bead-bound exosomes were washed three times with 200 μL of 2% BSA, followed by centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 2 minutes. Data were acquired using the Gallios 561(Beckman Coulter) and analyzed using FlowJo Ver 10.

Generation of Gal-3 KO GAC cell lines using Lenti-Crispr/Cas9
The CRISPR/Cas9 system was used to knock out Gal-3 in AGS and KP-Luc2 cell lines. Guide RNA design followed the principles listed on the Massachusetts Institute of Technology website (
http://crispr.mit.edu
) or German Cancer Research Center’s E-Crisp website (
http://www.e-crisp.org/E-CRISP/desighcrispr.html
). Guide RNAs for Gal-3 were inserted into V2mO (pLentiCrispr.V2. mOrange). Guide RNA sequences for Gal-3 KO are listed in
Table S9
. Briefly, 50 μL of each primer at 100μM were added together, and each pair of guide RNA sequences was formed into duplexes in a heating block heated to 100°C and cooled down to room temperature on its own. The duplexes were then used as inserts to ligate using T4 DNA ligase (NEB, Ipswich, MA) into V2mO (pLentiCrispr.V2mOrange) cut by BsmbI (NEB, Ipswich, MA). The ligates were transformed into Stabl3 competent cells, and resultant clones were screened by the size of inserts and verified by sequencing. Plasmids with the right inserts were then co-transfected with pCMV.Dr8.2 and pCMV-VSV.G at a ratio of 10:10:1 into HEK293T cells with 70% confluency using JetPrime (Polyplus, France). Supernatants were harvested 24 hours later, and consecutively two more times, 48 hours and 72 hours later. Lentiviral supernatants were centrifuged, and clear upper solution was filtered and used for immediate transduction or kept in a -80°C freezer for later use. Target AGS and KP-Luc2 GAC cells were seeded in a 6-well plate with 70% confluency, lentiviral supernatants were added with 8μM polybrene, and transduced cells were selected by puromycin at a concentration determined by killing curves for 3-6 days. Surviving cells were then subjected to single-cell cloning by FACS sorting or by dilution into 96-well plates. Positive clones were screened and verified by Western blot. Gal-3 cDNA in frame with 3xFlag marker was generated. Gal-3 cDNA generated by Q5 PCR with primers hGal3.XbaBamH.R with hGal3.g12.dg3.F3 was used to generate the p3xFlag-Gal3.dg3 plasmid. Clones were subjected to digestion and sequencing to verify that three nonconsecutive nucleotides were altered in the cDNAs of the gRNA1 binding site of the three plasmids.

Quantification and statistical analysis
Statistical analyses of flow cytometry and immunostaining quantifications were performed with one-way analysis of variance with the Tukey multiple comparison test, unpaired two-tailed
t

TCGA data were downloaded from cBioPortal. Kaplan-Meier plots were drawn for survival analysis and the log-rank Mantel-Cox test was used to evaluate statistical differences. A p value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Error bars represented standard error of the mean when multiple visual fields were averaged to produce a single value for each animal, which was then averaged again to represent the mean bar for the group in each graph.

Method details
Isolation of extracellular vesicles by density gradient flotation
Microvesicles were depleted from ascite samples by centrifugation at 2000 × g for 20 minutes, followed by 16,500 × g for 30 minutes; resulting supernatant was filtered through a pre-wetted 0.22-μm vacuum filter. Microvesicle-depleted biospecimens were densified by mixing with OptiPrep iodixanol solution (Sigma D1556) to a final density of 1.16-1.30 g/mL and loaded into the bottom of a polycarbonate ultracentrifuge tube and overlaid with 0.5- to 2-mL aliquots of iodixanol/phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) solution in the 1.20-1.01 g/mL (35-0% wt/vol) range, proceeding from the highest to lowest density to form a single- or multi-step density fractionation gradient as needed. Ultracentrifugation was performed at 100,000 ×
g
for 4 hours at 8°C. Vesicles were collected from the top of the tube, proceeding downward to recover volume equal to 90% of overlaid gradient volume. Density of harvested fractions was assessed against a standard curve based on sample absorbance at 250 nm using a NanoDrop microvolume spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Wilmington, DE). Vesicle harvests were stored at -80°C.
Proteomic profiling of extracellular vesicles
ECV-derived protein digestion and identification by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry was performed using established protocols. The nanoAcquity UPLC system coupled in-line with a WATERS SYNAPT G2-Si mass spectrometer was used for the separation of pooled digested protein fractions. The system was equipped with a Waters Symmetry C18 nanoAcquity trap-column (180 μm × 20 mm, 5 μm) and a Waters HSS-T3 C18 nanoAcquity analytical column (75 μm × 150 mm, 1.8 μm). The column oven temperature was set at 50°C, and the temperature of the tray compartment in the auto-sampler was set at 6°C. LC-HDMSE data were acquired in resolution mode with SYNAPT G2-Si using Waters Masslynx (version 4.1, SCN 851). The capillary voltage was set to 2.80 kV, sampling cone voltage to 30 V, source offset to 30 V, and source temperature to 100°C. Mobility used high-purity N2 as the drift gas in the IMS TriWave cell. The pressure was 4.50 mbar in the helium cell, 2.47 × 10
−2
mbar in the Trap cell, 2.90 mbar in the IMS TriWave cell, and 2.53 × 10
−3
mbar in the Transfer cell. IMS wave velocity was 600 m/s, helium cell DC 50 V, Trap DC bias 45 V, IMS TriWave DC bias 1 V, and IMS wave delay 1000 μs. The mass spectrometer was operated in V-mode with a typical resolving power of at least 20,000. All analyses were performed using positive mode ESI using a NanoLockSpray source. The lock mass channel was sampled every 60 seconds. The mass spectrometer was calibrated with a [Glu1] fibrinopeptide solution (300 fmol/μL) delivered through the reference sprayer of the NanoLockSpray source. Accurate mass LC-HDMSE data were collected in an alternating low-energy (MS) and high-energy (MSE) mode of acquisition with mass scan ranging from 50 m/z to 1800 m/z. The spectral acquisition time in each mode was 1.0 seconds with a 0.1-second inter-scan delay. In low-energy HDMS mode, data were collected at a constant collision energy of 2 eV in both the Trap cell and the Transfer cell. In high-energy HDMSE mode, the collision energy was ramped from 25 eV to 55 eV in the Transfer cell only. The RF applied to the quadrupole mass analyzer was adjusted such that ions from 300 m/z to 2000 m/z were efficiently transmitted, ensuring that any ions observed in the LC-HDMSE data <300 m/z arose from dissociations in the Transfer collision cell. The acquired LC-HDMSE data were processed and searched against a protein knowledge database (Uniprot) through the ProteinLynx Global Server (PLGS, Waters Company) with a 4% false discovery rate.
Exosome production from GAC cell line
The cells were cultured in serum-free medium for 48 hours at a confluency of 70-80% and washed twice with PBS. The conditioned medium was collected and followed by differential centrifugation at 800 × g for 5 minutes and 2,000 × g for 10 minutes, and then filtered using a 0.2-μm filter. Exosome isolation was performed by ultracentrifugation at 100,000 × g for 3 hours at 4°C. After ultracentrifugation, the supernatant was discarded, and the pellet was resuspended in PBS.
Nanoparticle tracking analysis
The size distribution of exosomes was determined based on the Brownian motion using a NanoSight LM10 (Malvern), which is equipped with a high-sensitivity sCMOS camera and Blue488 laser. The temperature was set at 25°C during measurement of exosomes. The syringe pump speed was set to 20. A 90-second delay followed by three captures of 30 seconds each was employed for each acquisition.
Transmission electron microscopy of exosomes
Exosomes were fixed in 2.5% EM grade glutaraldehyde. Formvar-carbon coated mesh nickel grids were treated with poly-l-lysine solution for 5 minutes, and excess was removed by the filter paper. The grids were allowed to dry. Drops of suspended exosomes were deposited on the formvar-carbon coated mesh nickel grids. Exosomes were adsorbed for 1 hour at room temperature. Grids were rinsed with PBS 5 times for 3 minutes each and incubated in filtered 1% uranyl acetate in distilled water for 1 minute. The excess was removed by filter paper, and grids were allowed to dry at room temperature. Grids were examined in a JEM 1010 transmission electron microscope (JEOL, USA, Inc, Peabody, MA) at 80 kV. Digital images were captured using the AMT Imaging System (Advanced Microscopy Techniques Corp, Danvers, MA).
Flow cytometry-based analysis of bead-bound exosomes
A total of 5 × 10
9
exosomes were resuspended in 100 μL of PBS and mixed with 10 μL of aldehyde/sulfate beads (Invitrogen). Then, the samples were incubated at room temperature with rotation for 15 minutes. Subsequently, exosomes were added with 400 μL of PBS and rotated overnight at 4°C. Samples were added to 200 μL of 1M glycine and rotated at room temperature for 1 hour on the following day. The bead-bound exosomes were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 2 minutes, the supernatant was discarded, and the samples were resuspended in 100 μL of 10% bovine serum albumin (BSA) for blocking and rotated at room temperature for 1 hour. After blocking, samples were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 2 minutes, supernatant was discarded, and the precipitate was resuspended in 50 μL of 2% BSA containing unconjugated primary antibodies CD9 (BD, Cat# 558749), CD63 (BD, Cat# 564221), and CD81 (BD, Cat# 559519). The samples were rotated at room temperature for 1 hour. Bead-bound exosomes were washed twice in 200 μL of 2% BSA, followed by centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 2 minutes. The supernatant was discarded, and bead-bound exosomes were rotated for 1 hour at room temperature with 20 μL of 2% BSA containing secondary antibody. Then the bead-bound exosomes were washed three times with 200 μL of 2% BSA, followed by centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 2 minutes. Data were acquired using the Gallios 561(Beckman Coulter) and analyzed using FlowJo Ver 10.

Briefly, 50 μL of each primer at 100μM were added together, and each pair of guide RNA sequences was formed into duplexes in a heating block heated to 100°C and cooled down to room temperature on its own. Introduction
Peritoneal carcinomatosis (PC; also called malignant ascites, or implants in the peritoneal cavity) from gastric adenocarcinoma (GAC) is associated with poor patient survival (≤6 months).
1
The dismal prognosis is due to the suboptimal therapeutic landscape and inherent therapy resistance.
2
Incorporation of immunotherapy has benefited only a small subset of patients.
3
,
4
Lack of novel therapeutics for PC is a major unmet need in the clinic. Therefore, deep dives into the molecular mechanisms of PC and immunology could uncover therapeutic targets.
Several reports suggest that cancer cells secrete many factors for self-sustaining proliferation and release exosomes that remodel the tumor microenvironment for successful dissemination.
5
,
6
,
7
,
8
,
9
,
10
,
11
,
12
,
13
Exosomes promote lung, liver, and brain metastases by modulating the microenvironment, which involves the modification of endothelial cells to allow vascular leakiness and activation of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) to create a tumor-promoting microenvironment.
5
,
9
Exosomes also promote PC by disrupting the mesothelial barrier, thus promoting adhesion to mesothelial cells and leading to mesothelial-mesenchymal transition in GAC.
14
,
15
Nevertheless, the precise molecular and mechanistic contributions of exosomes to PC in the ecosystem of the peritoneal cavity remain unclear.
Galectin-3 (Gal-3) in tumors has been implicated in cancer progression and metastasis through cell proliferation, growth, and immune responses.
16
However, cancer cell-derived exosomal Gal-3 in the pre-metastasis stage is less understood. In the current study, using in-depth proteomic profiling of exosomes derived from PC, we identified Gal-3 as the payload in exosomes. Gal-3 contributed to the immunosuppressive microenvironment through CAF activation, which was associated with the dysfunction of T cells. Perturbation of exosomal Gal-3 and other related molecules considerably reduced PC, suggesting a potential therapeutic targeting strategy for PC in GAC.

Discussion
A common metastatic site of GAC is the peritoneal cavity.
28
PC affects ∼45% of patients with GAC , who often have a short survival duration of ≤6 months.
29
,
30
Therefore, new therapeutic targets coupled with ablative technologies are widely anticipated to lessen or eliminate the onset of PC and prolong PC patient survival, but new therapeutic targets must first be identified. In the current study, we explored the role of exosome cargo in cancer progression and the function of exosomes in organotrophic metastases in GAC.
Previous reports have shown that tumor cells remodulate the microenvironment of a target organ that would support successful metastatic colonization.
5
,
6
,
7
,
9
,
10
,
11
,
12
,
17
,
31
,
32
Among tumor-secreted factors, tumor-derived exosomes are crucial players in cell-to-cell communication, and exosomes reshape distant microenvironments, driving organ-specific metastases.
9
,
32
Exosomes engage in multiple systemic pathophysiologic processes, such as reprogramming stromal recipient cells and regulating and suppressing anticancer immunity, to establish supportive interactions with organ-specific niches and subsequent metastases.
17
Several reports indicate that exosomes play this role in lung, liver, and brain metastases, consolidating the principles of exosome-mediated microenvironment modulation.
7
,
9
,
12
,
33
,
34
,
35
,
36
Several groups have reported that exosomes promote PC by destroying the mesothelial barrier and initiating tumor invasion into the peritoneal cavity in both GAC and ovarian cancer.
37
,
38
Others have reported that GAC-derived exosomes promote cancer cell adhesion to mesothelial cells or induce mesothelial-mesenchymal transition.
39
,
40
Although previous studies have shown that extracellular Gal-3 promotes tumor invasiveness and Gal-3, expressed in cancer cells, inhibits cancer metastasis in melanoma. However, it is important to note that extracellular Gal-3 and cancer cells Gal-3 differs from exosomal Gal-3.
41
,
42
While several studies have shown the presence of Gal-3 in exosomes from bladder and colon cancer,
43
,
44
the specific function of exosomal Gal-3 has not been thoroughly explored. Additionally, the role of exosomal Gal-3 may vary across different tumor types, highlighting the need for a tumor-specific investigation of its functional role. In the current study, we used multi-omics analyses combined with patient-derived orthotopic and syngeneic mouse models to reveal that exosomal Gal-3 induced CAF activation to form a fibroblast niche, which further suppressed T cell function in the peritoneal cavity.
Our research echoes similar findings observed in other contexts, particularly in the realm of gastric cancer. Building upon the strides made in pancreatic cancer research regarding the efficacy of CXCL12/CXCR4 and anti-PD-1 therapies, our investigation sought to determine whether analogous strategies hold promise for the treatment of GAC. Our study pioneered the isolation and characterization of exosomes extracted from the ascites of patients afflicted with GAC. Employing cutting-edge mass spectrometry techniques, we identified Gal-3 as a prominent component of these ascites-derived exosomes. Noteworthy parallels emerge with previous studies that have highlighted the role of Gal-3 in orchestrating cellular processes, including myofibroblast activation and extracellular matrix modulation, albeit in non-neoplastic conditions.
Central to our findings is the conspicuous overexpression of Gal-3 on both cancer cells and cancer-derived exosomes within the GAC milieu. Functionally, exosomal Gal-3 emerges as a key protagonist in driving GAC progression by fostering CAF activation, instigating niche formation, and dampening antitumor immune responses within the peritoneal cavity. This discovery not only provides valuable insights into the dynamic remodeling of the peritoneal microenvironment but also unveils potential therapeutic targets with implications for GAC management. At the mechanistic level, our investigations unveil a signaling cascade wherein exosomal Gal-3–induced CAF activation proceeds through the integrin α1β1/FAK/Akt/mTOR/CXCL12 axis. Notably, the consequential dysregulation of the CXCL12/CXCR4 pathway exacerbates the immunosuppressive milieu within the peritoneal cavity by impeding T cell mobilization and cytotoxic functions. These findings underscore the intricate interplay between exosomal cargo, stromal components, and immune effectors, thereby delineating promising avenues for therapeutic intervention in GAC akin to those observed in PC. A limitation of our current study is the lack of investigation into the origin of CAFs and the role of exosomal Gal-3 in mesothelial to mesenchymal transition which has been demonstrated as a resource of CAF in previous studies.
39
,
45
,
46
This is an important aspect that warrants further exploration in our future studies.
In summary, our results showed that exosomal Gal-3 remodels the microenvironment, promoting the progression of PC. CAF activation triggers an immunosuppressive microenvironment through CXCL12 secretion. Additionally, simultaneous inhibition of exosomal Gal-3, CXCR4, and PD-1 produces the most striking PC suppression, which has implications for developing rational therapeutic strategies.

A limitation of our current study is the lack of investigation into the origin of CAFs and the role of exosomal Gal-3 in mesothelial to mesenchymal transition which has been demonstrated as a resource of CAF in previous studies.

Experimental model and study participant details
Cells and reagents
The human gastric cancer cell line AGS was purchased from American Type Culture Collection. The KP-Luc2 murine GAC cell line was from the laboratory of Dr. Jo Ishizawa in the Department of Leukemia at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center (Houston, TX). All cell lines were profiled, authenticated, and Mycoplasma-tested in the Cell Line Core Facility at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center every 6 months. TD-139 was from Selleck Chem (Cat# S0471), neutralizing PD-1 antibody was from Bio X Cell (Cat# BE0146), AMD3100 was from Selleckchem (Cat# S8030), and FAK inhibitor PND-1186 was from Selleckchem (Cat# S7653).

Ex vivo
assays with human T cells
Patient ascites lymphocytes were isolated from Buffy Coats using Ficoll PAQUE (GE Healthcare) and were cryopreserved until further use. After thawing, patient ascites lymphocytes were cultured in RPMI 1640 (Corning) supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% penicillin-streptomycin, and 50μM β-mercapoethanol for 48 hours. T cells were treated with 1 μg/mL anti-CD3e (BioLegend) and 1 μg/mL anti-CD28 (eBioscience) for 24 hours, followed by exosome treatment for another 48 hours. Cells were incubated with the human antibodies CD45 (BioLegend, Cat# 982316), CD3 (BD, Cat# 557832), CD8 (BD Bioscience, Cat# 557945), and Granzyme B (BD, Cat# 563389). Data were acquired using Gallios 561 (Beckman Coulter) and analyzed using FlowJo Ver 10.
Patient-derived orthotopic model
Mouse work was performed in accordance with Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and AAALAS guidelines (MD Anderson animal protocol 00000232-RN03), and the study was compliant with all relevant ethical regulations regarding animal research. 10 μg exosomes were intraperitoneally injected into the 8-12 weeks female SCID mice peritoneal cavity 3 times per week for 2 weeks. For the orthotopic injection, SCID mice were first anesthetized with isoflurane inhalation and then laid in a supine position. A 6- to 10-mm incision was made in the midline of the mouse abdomen, and the stomach was exteriorized with forceps. Then, 1 × 10
5
GA0518 cells with mCherry-Luciferase in 30 μL of matrigel were injected into the subserosal layer of the stomach with a 27-gauge needle. The stomach was returned into the abdominal cavity and the skin was closed with wound clips. Tumor growth and PC were monitored every week through bioluminescence imaging of surgery mice.

For experimental exosome education, exosomes (10 μg) were intraperitoneally injected 3 times per week for 2 weeks. 8-12 weeks female C57BL/6 mice were the intraperitoneally injected with 1 × 10

Method details
Isolation of extracellular vesicles by density gradient flotation
Microvesicles were depleted from ascite samples by centrifugation at 2000 × g for 20 minutes, followed by 16,500 × g for 30 minutes; resulting supernatant was filtered through a pre-wetted 0.22-μm vacuum filter. Microvesicle-depleted biospecimens were densified by mixing with OptiPrep iodixanol solution (Sigma D1556) to a final density of 1.16-1.30 g/mL and loaded into the bottom of a polycarbonate ultracentrifuge tube and overlaid with 0.5- to 2-mL aliquots of iodixanol/phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) solution in the 1.20-1.01 g/mL (35-0% wt/vol) range, proceeding from the highest to lowest density to form a single- or multi-step density fractionation gradient as needed. Ultracentrifugation was performed at 100,000 ×
g
for 4 hours at 8°C. Vesicles were collected from the top of the tube, proceeding downward to recover volume equal to 90% of overlaid gradient volume. Density of harvested fractions was assessed against a standard curve based on sample absorbance at 250 nm using a NanoDrop microvolume spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Wilmington, DE). Vesicle harvests were stored at -80°C.
Proteomic profiling of extracellular vesicles
ECV-derived protein digestion and identification by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry was performed using established protocols. The nanoAcquity UPLC system coupled in-line with a WATERS SYNAPT G2-Si mass spectrometer was used for the separation of pooled digested protein fractions. The system was equipped with a Waters Symmetry C18 nanoAcquity trap-column (180 μm × 20 mm, 5 μm) and a Waters HSS-T3 C18 nanoAcquity analytical column (75 μm × 150 mm, 1.8 μm). The column oven temperature was set at 50°C, and the temperature of the tray compartment in the auto-sampler was set at 6°C. LC-HDMSE data were acquired in resolution mode with SYNAPT G2-Si using Waters Masslynx (version 4.1, SCN 851). The capillary voltage was set to 2.80 kV, sampling cone voltage to 30 V, source offset to 30 V, and source temperature to 100°C. Mobility used high-purity N2 as the drift gas in the IMS TriWave cell. The pressure was 4.50 mbar in the helium cell, 2.47 × 10
−2
mbar in the Trap cell, 2.90 mbar in the IMS TriWave cell, and 2.53 × 10
−3
mbar in the Transfer cell. IMS wave velocity was 600 m/s, helium cell DC 50 V, Trap DC bias 45 V, IMS TriWave DC bias 1 V, and IMS wave delay 1000 μs. The mass spectrometer was operated in V-mode with a typical resolving power of at least 20,000. All analyses were performed using positive mode ESI using a NanoLockSpray source. The lock mass channel was sampled every 60 seconds. The mass spectrometer was calibrated with a [Glu1] fibrinopeptide solution (300 fmol/μL) delivered through the reference sprayer of the NanoLockSpray source. Accurate mass LC-HDMSE data were collected in an alternating low-energy (MS) and high-energy (MSE) mode of acquisition with mass scan ranging from 50 m/z to 1800 m/z. The spectral acquisition time in each mode was 1.0 seconds with a 0.1-second inter-scan delay. In low-energy HDMS mode, data were collected at a constant collision energy of 2 eV in both the Trap cell and the Transfer cell. In high-energy HDMSE mode, the collision energy was ramped from 25 eV to 55 eV in the Transfer cell only. The RF applied to the quadrupole mass analyzer was adjusted such that ions from 300 m/z to 2000 m/z were efficiently transmitted, ensuring that any ions observed in the LC-HDMSE data <300 m/z arose from dissociations in the Transfer collision cell. The acquired LC-HDMSE data were processed and searched against a protein knowledge database (Uniprot) through the ProteinLynx Global Server (PLGS, Waters Company) with a 4% false discovery rate.
Exosome production from GAC cell line
The cells were cultured in serum-free medium for 48 hours at a confluency of 70-80% and washed twice with PBS. The conditioned medium was collected and followed by differential centrifugation at 800 × g for 5 minutes and 2,000 × g for 10 minutes, and then filtered using a 0.2-μm filter. Exosome isolation was performed by ultracentrifugation at 100,000 × g for 3 hours at 4°C. After ultracentrifugation, the supernatant was discarded, and the pellet was resuspended in PBS.
Nanoparticle tracking analysis
The size distribution of exosomes was determined based on the Brownian motion using a NanoSight LM10 (Malvern), which is equipped with a high-sensitivity sCMOS camera and Blue488 laser. The temperature was set at 25°C during measurement of exosomes. The syringe pump speed was set to 20. A 90-second delay followed by three captures of 30 seconds each was employed for each acquisition.
Transmission electron microscopy of exosomes
Exosomes were fixed in 2.5% EM grade glutaraldehyde. Formvar-carbon coated mesh nickel grids were treated with poly-l-lysine solution for 5 minutes, and excess was removed by the filter paper. The grids were allowed to dry. Drops of suspended exosomes were deposited on the formvar-carbon coated mesh nickel grids. Exosomes were adsorbed for 1 hour at room temperature. Grids were rinsed with PBS 5 times for 3 minutes each and incubated in filtered 1% uranyl acetate in distilled water for 1 minute. The excess was removed by filter paper, and grids were allowed to dry at room temperature. Grids were examined in a JEM 1010 transmission electron microscope (JEOL, USA, Inc, Peabody, MA) at 80 kV. Digital images were captured using the AMT Imaging System (Advanced Microscopy Techniques Corp, Danvers, MA).
Flow cytometry-based analysis of bead-bound exosomes
A total of 5 × 10
9
exosomes were resuspended in 100 μL of PBS and mixed with 10 μL of aldehyde/sulfate beads (Invitrogen). Then, the samples were incubated at room temperature with rotation for 15 minutes. Subsequently, exosomes were added with 400 μL of PBS and rotated overnight at 4°C. Samples were added to 200 μL of 1M glycine and rotated at room temperature for 1 hour on the following day. The bead-bound exosomes were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 2 minutes, the supernatant was discarded, and the samples were resuspended in 100 μL of 10% bovine serum albumin (BSA) for blocking and rotated at room temperature for 1 hour. After blocking, samples were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 2 minutes, supernatant was discarded, and the precipitate was resuspended in 50 μL of 2% BSA containing unconjugated primary antibodies CD9 (BD, Cat# 558749), CD63 (BD, Cat# 564221), and CD81 (BD, Cat# 559519). The samples were rotated at room temperature for 1 hour. Bead-bound exosomes were washed twice in 200 μL of 2% BSA, followed by centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 2 minutes. The supernatant was discarded, and bead-bound exosomes were rotated for 1 hour at room temperature with 20 μL of 2% BSA containing secondary antibody. Then the bead-bound exosomes were washed three times with 200 μL of 2% BSA, followed by centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 2 minutes. Data were acquired using the Gallios 561(Beckman Coulter) and analyzed using FlowJo Ver 10.

Generation of Gal-3 KO GAC cell lines using Lenti-Crispr/Cas9
The CRISPR/Cas9 system was used to knock out Gal-3 in AGS and KP-Luc2 cell lines. Guide RNA design followed the principles listed on the Massachusetts Institute of Technology website (
http://crispr.mit.edu
) or German Cancer Research Center’s E-Crisp website (
http://www.e-crisp.org/E-CRISP/desighcrispr.html
). Guide RNAs for Gal-3 were inserted into V2mO (pLentiCrispr.V2. mOrange). Guide RNA sequences for Gal-3 KO are listed in
Table S9
. Briefly, 50 μL of each primer at 100μM were added together, and each pair of guide RNA sequences was formed into duplexes in a heating block heated to 100°C and cooled down to room temperature on its own. The duplexes were then used as inserts to ligate using T4 DNA ligase (NEB, Ipswich, MA) into V2mO (pLentiCrispr.V2mOrange) cut by BsmbI (NEB, Ipswich, MA). The ligates were transformed into Stabl3 competent cells, and resultant clones were screened by the size of inserts and verified by sequencing. Plasmids with the right inserts were then co-transfected with pCMV.Dr8.2 and pCMV-VSV.G at a ratio of 10:10:1 into HEK293T cells with 70% confluency using JetPrime (Polyplus, France). Supernatants were harvested 24 hours later, and consecutively two more times, 48 hours and 72 hours later. Lentiviral supernatants were centrifuged, and clear upper solution was filtered and used for immediate transduction or kept in a -80°C freezer for later use. Target AGS and KP-Luc2 GAC cells were seeded in a 6-well plate with 70% confluency, lentiviral supernatants were added with 8μM polybrene, and transduced cells were selected by puromycin at a concentration determined by killing curves for 3-6 days. Surviving cells were then subjected to single-cell cloning by FACS sorting or by dilution into 96-well plates. Positive clones were screened and verified by Western blot. Gal-3 cDNA in frame with 3xFlag marker was generated. Gal-3 cDNA generated by Q5 PCR with primers hGal3.XbaBamH.R with hGal3.g12.dg3.F3 was used to generate the p3xFlag-Gal3.dg3 plasmid. Clones were subjected to digestion and sequencing to verify that three nonconsecutive nucleotides were altered in the cDNAs of the gRNA1 binding site of the three plasmids.

Quantification and statistical analysis
Statistical analyses of flow cytometry and immunostaining quantifications were performed with one-way analysis of variance with the Tukey multiple comparison test, unpaired two-tailed
t
test, or Fisher exact test using GraphPad Prism (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA). Expression levels of indicated genes among TCGA STAD cohort samples were based on the RNA Seq V2 RSEM data. TCGA data were downloaded from cBioPortal. Kaplan-Meier plots were drawn for survival analysis and the log-rank Mantel-Cox test was used to evaluate statistical differences. A p value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Error bars represented standard error of the mean when multiple visual fields were averaged to produce a single value for each animal, which was then averaged again to represent the mean bar for the group in each graph.
